children: By Anna Silman | Illustration by Ricardo Tomás for WSJ. Magazine
WSJ. MAGAZINE

DAN FUGARDI has always been careful about what he puts online. He rarely posts photos of himself and avoids sharing his location, with a vigilance that harks back to his time as a nuclear engineer in the U.S. Navy. And on first dates, he asks that his romantic prospects please put away their phones.

"You go out with somebody you don't know, and you're risking throwing communications out into the ether that are potentially there forever," says Fugardi, a serial executive who now runs a hair-tool business. "It's almost reckless, as a shepherd of a company."

This past week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after two extramarital affairs came to light: one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with an employee. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment. But in the age of 24/7 surveillance, an executive need not be Huang-, Musk- or Bezos-level famous to become infamous for personal matters. Consider the case of former Astronomer CEO Andy Byron, forced to resign after being caught embracing the company's HR head at a Coldplay concert, or the New York City law partner who left his firm after a TikToker captured him smooching an associate in Central Park. Today's corporate leaders are more visible and scrutinized than ever before, and their reputations are inextricable from the fortunes of the companies they represent.

"Privacy, privilege, spontaneity — that's become more and more of a rarefied position," says Don Aviv, a security consultant for high-net-worth individuals who runs the business intelligence and investigative firm Interfor International. "Just being the CEO of a company or an executive puts you in that spotlight."

One need not cross ethical lines to inadvertently become X's main character: Every digital-age romance comes with its own trove of potentially embarrassing material just waiting to tumble out into the open. Add to that the rise in scams, thefts and data breaches targeting CEOs, and you can see why they are turning to teams of experts in hopes that matters of the heart can be managed just like any other aspect of their investment portfolios.

"I'm there to protect them because we can't get this wrong," says Amy Andersen, who helps set up tech executives via her Menlo Park, California-based firm, Linx Dating. "There's way too much to risk."

ANDERSEN IS PART of an elite cadre of romantic intermediaries whose services are getting more expensive by the minute; data from DateSpot shows that the average cost of matchmaking rose 26% between January 2025 and 2026.

She begins by looking through her encrypted database of potential matches to find someone who aligns with the client's desires. These individuals then undergo an intensive vetting process, complete with NDAs. Her goal is to create "a controlled dating ecosystem" in which she acts as a "bodyguard" for her clients. Her rates start at $75,000 and can hit half a million.

Matchmakers go to great lengths to conceal their clients' identities ahead of a first meeting. Their dates sometimes receive scrambled biographical details and fake look-alike photos. Even on the actual date, some matchmakers advise clients to downplay their status.
"I had a client who drove a Maserati, and we put a strategy in place that he would rent and drive a Prius to pick up his first date," says Rachel Greenwald of Greenwald Executive Matchmaking.

Green flags include keeping a low profile and being willing to go dark on social media, according to Cody Shultz, who leads Private Client Protection at intelligence firm Guidepost Solutions. A common scenario is when an executive with a deliberately limited online profile begins dating someone with fewer digital boundaries.

"If the person's already showing that they are just talking about everything online, they've got a very open social media presence, that may be enough to have the executive decide that this isn't the right play," Shultz says.
Though that's not always how things happen in reality, according to Alex Wolf, founder of OnlyFnds, which provides financial services for OnlyFans models.

"You may have a high-profile individual who is like, 'I don't want to date an influencer; keep her away from me if she has over 10,000 followers,' but the reality is they still pursue the exact archetype of woman they're saying they don't want," she says.

FOR EXECUTIVES SEEKING ROMANCE, visibility is a double-edged sword. Not only do they have to worry about privacy, but their own high profiles can also mean it's challenging to meet someone who hasn't already formed preconceptions about them.

"There's no more magic in a first date," says Bryan Goldberg, CEO and founder of the media company BDG. "KKR's legal department cannot perform diligence at the level of a single woman on a first date."
In turn, some executives enlist investigative firms and reputation-management services to compile dossiers on prospective lovers.

"There used to be a push for understanding any sort of civil or criminal litigation history," says Shultz, who previously worked as a CIA officer. "Now it's changed to be much more of a stress on reputation."

Aviv, the security consultant, typically charges $4,000 on top of his standard rate to conduct research into a potential romantic partner. That involves everything from reviewing past social media posts to combing through litigation history.

Executive anxiety is at an all-time high, he notes, particularly after events like the shooting of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson by Luigi Mangione and the Molotov cocktail-style attack on OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's home. With the boom in AI and facial recognition, this can also involve making sure that the potential partner isn't involved in any sort of hot-button social or political issue that could compromise the executive's reputation.
"Much of it is the same advice we give to these wealthy individuals before a business transaction: Vet and verify," Aviv says.

Security is especially a concern for high-profile female clients. One of Aviv's clients, an executive at a private-equity firm in New England, has him investigate every prospective date. His job also frequently involves fighting hackers who have stolen clients' "boudoir shots" as well as hunting for deepfakes.

The worst-case scenario is what he calls "honeypot situations," which can impact both genders, where someone is planted to steal money or corporate information under the guise of a romantic relationship. While it may sound like something out of Homeland, it's a topic big tech firms are thinking about: OpenAI recently held training sessions warning employees about spies trying to access company data, including honeypots. Huang's affair with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence has quickly become an industry cautionary tale.

"PRIVACY USED TO BE about avoiding one photographer or avoiding a couple of photographers that stood outside the executive or celebrity's regular haunt," says Greenwald. Now it's all about "controlling the room."

The modern-day paparazzo isn't hiding in the bushes outside Chateau Marmont; it's the person at the next table surreptitiously filming on their phone or a pair of smartglasses. Increased surveillance in public spaces — from Flock cameras on highways to facial recognition technology at stadiums — has made it harder than ever to go about life incognito. As a result, private members' clubs have become a go-to safe space.

Within the cosseted walls of ZZs and Chez Margaux, concierge services and matchmakers do everything from making sure the table is far enough away from its neighbors to coordinating separate entrances.
"We're finding the private members' clubs are the places where it all begins," says Stuart McNeill, who often plans dates for clients via his luxury travel and concierge service Knightsbridge Circle.

Sometimes he has to get more creative. McNeill once arranged for two recognizable individuals to go on a date to a private suite at a stadium concert. To make sure they weren't spotted when they were out on the balcony, he hired people to fill the booth so it would seem like a group hang instead of on a one-on-one date.

Other solutions are lower-fi. Greenwald says that often instead of selecting a Michelin-star restaurant, she'll select a casual neighborhood cafe on a Tuesday night rather than a Saturday night. Another option is eating at home — or something resembling home. Before she met her husband, investor Elena Nuñez says she would have her security advisor rent Airbnbs so dates could come over and cook dinner in a more intimate setting, while still not disclosing her personal address.

Erica Arrechea of Cinque Matchmaking once had a client who owned an oil company and couldn't find time in his schedule for a night out. Plus, he didn't drink. The solution? They met for a glass of water around 3 p.m. "It's probably the unsexiest way to have a date," she says. "But nine months later, they were engaged."
NO MATTER how new and shiny a relationship is, for some execs it's never too early to start worrying about the end.
Just look at the ongoing divorce proceedings between hedge-fund founder John Overdeck and his wife, Laura, the outcome of which risks upending the power balance within his firm's C-suite.

Divorce lawyer Bob Cohen, of firm Cohen Clair Lans Greifer & Simpson LLP, has represented Melinda French Gates and Georgina Chapman. He says he prepares about 25 "cohabitation agreements" a year for top executives, which are legal documents that preserve an individual's right to remove a significant other from their shared residence.

Lawyer Jacqueline Newman, who specializes in complex divorce cases, says she has seen an uptick in clients seeking contracts at earlier points in their relationship, especially if they are paying for a partner's major expenses. "They don't want those payments or even the relationship to be something that could create any legal obligation," she says.

To get out ahead of potential issues, lawyers advise clients to inform their boards whenever they enter a new relationship — particularly if there's an extramarital affair or if they've fallen in love with a colleague (both more common than you'd think). In 2023, BP CEO Bernard Looney resigned after admitting he had not been "fully transparent" about "historical relationships with colleagues." Last year, Nestlé CEO Laurent Freixe was dismissed after an investigation into what the company called "an undisclosed romantic relationship with a direct subordinate"; a representative for Freixe said he contests both the grounds and the manner of his dismissal. Research by University of Denver management professor Michael Nalick shows executives are nearly five times more likely to be fired for personal misconduct than financial misconduct.
"If it's a public company, it could adversely affect the stock price, so it's very much an important issue for a senior executive to deal with," says Cohen.
With so many hoops to jump through, some CEOs find themselves avoiding romance altogether — especially the new class of AI founders coming to Andersen for help.
"They literally do not leave work," she says. "They are painfully single."
